Caveat

KAV-ee-at -- three syllables, stress on KAV. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Caveat is a specific warning or condition attached to something.

The lease looked generous, but it came with one caveat: the landlord could raise the rent after a single year.

Worked Example

The scholarship letter congratulates her warmly, then adds in bold print that the award applies only if she maintains a B-plus average every semester.

That attached condition -- a specific 'but be aware' clause built into the offer -- is a caveat. A caveat is a formal warning or stipulation that limits how far a promise, offer, or claim extends.

How Caveat Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

proviso

proviso: a condition attached to an agreement

stipulation

stipulation: a specific requirement spelled out in a deal

Antonyms

guarantee

guarantee: an unconditional promise

assurance

assurance: a confident statement meant to remove doubt

How Strong Is It? — proviso → caveat → warning

proviso vs. caveat

proviso vs. caveat: Proviso is drier and more neutral than caveat -- a proviso is simply a condition written into an agreement, while a caveat adds a note of warning: pay attention, or this could go wrong.

warning vs. caveat

warning vs. caveat: Warning is blunter and more urgent than caveat: a caveat is a measured condition attached to an offer or claim, while a warning points straight at danger and demands immediate attention.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cav-/caut-

root — cav-/caut-: to beware, be on guard (Latin cavere)

Put it together

Put it together: Caveat is a whole Latin verb form borrowed intact: it literally means 'let him beware,' from cavere, 'to beware, be on guard.' A caveat is the beware-clause of an offer or claim -- the part that tells you exactly what to watch out for.

Use the root in a new word: precaution

Use the root in a new word: precaution: As a precaution, the crew checked every rope twice before beginning the climb.

Root Check

Word Choice

Caveat appears in patterns like 'with the caveat that...' and 'one caveat:' -- and survives in the legal Latin phrase caveat emptor, 'let the buyer beware.' Keep it for specific, stated warnings or conditions attached to an offer, plan, or claim -- not as a vague synonym for 'problem.'
